Which Fish Can Live Together in a Community Fish Tank?
Help! My Fish Are Fighting: A Guide to Restoring Peace in Your Tank

facts.fact: Aquatic veterinarian Jessica Allen advises thinking about how tank mates will get along when planning a new tank, because fish do best with little stress and little competition.
Melissa Witherell, DVM, advises researching every species before stocking, so that the fish come from similar regions and need similar water conditions.
Before buying, look up whether each species you are considering is compatible with the others.
Overcrowding can stress even peaceful fish.

Causes of fighting include territorial behaviour (made worse by too few hiding places or newly added fish), fin nippers kept with long-finned fish, competition for food, breeding behaviour, and a tank too small for the fishes' adult size.
Tiger barbs are known for nipping fins, but this is mainly a problem when too few are kept or space is limited.
Keep tiger barbs in a group of at least 8–10, which spreads their aggression among themselves.
Barbs are shoaling fish and should be kept in groups of at least five, with more being better. Larger groups help reduce fin nipping.
Do not keep tiger barbs with timid, slow-moving or long-finned fish, such as many livebearers, cichlids and anabantoids.
The best tank mates for tiger barbs are robust, similarly sized cyprinids that swim in open water. Some loaches and bottom-dwelling cyprinids such as Crossocheilus or Garra are also suitable.
Barbs should not be mixed with slow-swimming, timid or long-finned fish. Larger barb species should not be kept with fish small enough to fit in their mouths.
Cherry, six-banded and checker barbs are generally fine with other peaceful species.
Do not keep tiger barbs with long-finned fish such as guppies.
Seriously Fish describes ornamental strains of Betta splendens as more aggressive than any other Betta species. In most cases only one can be kept per tank.
Male and female bettas are usually kept apart except for breeding.
Seriously Fish does not recommend Betta splendens for a standard community aquarium. Some small cyprinids and loaches from similar habitats can work, but this is the exception, not the norm.
Avoid keeping fish with trailing fins or unusual body shapes with a male betta, because he may treat them as rivals.
Chewy suggests a tank of more than 20 gallons for keeping a betta with other species.
Chewy says cichlids are aggressive and should be kept out of community tanks, and that dwarf gouramis can become territorial.
Mollies kept in small tanks need more space and may become aggressive.
Keep tetras in groups of at least six.
Signs of fighting or bullying include one fish repeatedly chasing another, ramming, shredded or torn fins, missing scales or wounds, a victim that hides most of the time, and refusal to eat.
Isolate the aggressor for a while to reduce its dominance and give injured fish time to recover. It may start fighting again when put back.
Test ammonia, nitrite, nitrate and temperature, because poor water conditions can make fish more irritable.
Consider separating fish permanently if they are repeatedly injured, if the aggression is constant, or if one fish stops the others from feeding.
To reduce fighting, rearrange the rocks, wood and decor to break up existing territories, add caves and dense plants, and block lines of sight.
Feed in several spots and use sinking food for bottom dwellers, so that fast eaters do not dominate.
Skin injuries make it harder for a fish to regulate its salt and water balance, and serious wounds can cause fluid loss and circulatory collapse.
The Merck Veterinary Manual strongly recommends quarantining new fish, for at least 30 days.
Chewy suggests quarantining new fish for 4 to 6 weeks.
In Vietnam the betta is sold as 'cá xiêm', and Corydoras as 'cá chuột'. The harlequin rasbora is called 'cá tam giác'.
Vietnamese shops call the guppy 'cá 7 màu' or 'cá bảy màu', platies 'cá bình tích' and Otocinclus 'cá otto'.
